draft.title: Pliny the Younger's letters
card: Pliny the Younger was a Roman writer and official. He was about 17 and at Misenum, across the Bay of Naples, when Vesuvius erupted in AD 79.
Years later, the historian Tacitus asked him for an account. Pliny replied in two letters: one on the death of his uncle, Pliny the Elder, and one on his own experience.
Pliny the Elder was a naval commander and writer. He sailed towards the eruption to rescue people and died on the shore at Stabiae.
The letters are the only surviving written account by someone who saw the eruption. They were written about 25 years later, from memory, so they have limits as evidence.
draft.remember: Pliny's two letters to Tacitus are our only eyewitness written account, but he wrote them long after the event.

a.q: Why are Pliny the Younger's letters important to historians of the eruption?
opts: They are the only surviving written account by an eyewitness
They were written on the day of the eruption itself
They describe the destruction of Pompeii street by street
They were written by Tacitus as an official report
a.why: Pliny saw the eruption from Misenum, and no other written account by an eyewitness survives. The letters were not written on the day: he wrote them years later when Tacitus asked, and Tacitus was the person receiving them.
a.clue: Think about who saw the eruption and put it in writing.

b.q: A student says Pliny's letters give a perfectly reliable record of the eruption. Which reason best shows the weakness in this claim?
opts: He wrote them about 25 years later, from memory
He was in Rome and only heard about the eruption
He wrote them to the emperor to praise Vesuvius
He wrote about his uncle only and not about himself
b.why: The letters were written long after AD 79, so memory and the purpose of the account may have shaped what he said. He was an eyewitness at Misenum, not in Rome, and the two letters covered both his uncle's death and his own experience.
b.clue: Check how much time passed between the eruption and the writing.
